title: Benedict
hookLine: a young man flees Rome's chaos for a cave, then writes a rule of life for monks
carry: listen, with the ear of the heart

lines: BREAD ON A ROPE, AND A BELL.
cards: Bread comes down on a rope, with a little bell tied on so the man below will know it's coming. He's living alone in a cave in the hills, and a monk nearby keeps him fed.

Not long before, he was a student in Rome, from a good family. He looked at the city, and at the students around him, and was afraid that if he stayed, he'd go over the same edge they were going over.
So he walked away from his books and his prospects. The young man is Benedict.

teach.b: His early life comes from Gregory the Great, a pope who wrote it down in a book of stories called the Dialogues. Gregory's Benedict is full of wonders.
But what Benedict himself left behind is quieter: a Rule, a short book about how monks should live together. Here's how it begins, in its Latin: Ausculta, o fili.
Listen, my son, to the master's teaching, and incline the ear of your heart.
Listen is the first word. Not obey. Not work.
Listen, and with the ear of the heart. The Rule keeps turning to scripture. Early on it takes up a psalm, in the King James words: "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart."
Then it gets practical. When to pray, through the day and the night. When to eat, how much, and when to keep silent.
How to choose an abbot, and why the abbot should call everyone to counsel, even the youngest, because, the Rule says, the Lord often shows what is better to the younger.
How to welcome guests: each one received as Christ, because Christ will say, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." The Rule hopes to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.

It calls itself a little rule for beginners. One thing often said about Benedict isn't his: the motto ora et labora, pray and work. It's a fair summary of the life, but those words aren't in the Rule.
What's in the Rule is the first word, and communities that follow it, Catholic, Anglican and others, still read from it together.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns, in Catholic, Anglican and other communities, live by the Rule of Benedict and read from it together, and some lay Christians follow its pattern of prayer, work and hospitality as oblates.

o: a pope who wrote a book of stories about saints
a monk whose Rule for living begins with listen
a hermit who lived alone in a cave all his life

games.q: what's inside the Rule — tap the pairs.
p: how the Rule asks you to listen

s: ora et labora, pray and work, is a line in Benedict's Rule
it's a later summary of the life. the Rule's first word is listen.
the Rule says guests are to be received as Christ
because Christ will say, I was a stranger, and ye took me in.
the Rule calls itself a demanding rule for experts
it calls itself a little rule for beginners, and hopes for nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.

games.q: you're young, studying in Rome, and you don't like who the city is making you. what do you do?
o: stay, and try to fit in.
leave your studies for a life of prayer.
stay, and keep your head down.
games.why: Gregory says Benedict left his studies and the city, and ended up in a cave, fed by a monk's bread on a rope.

practice: Start where Benedict starts: listen, and ask what the ear of your heart is hearing about how your days are going.

Maybe it's more sleep, one meal without a screen, a few quiet minutes in the morning; let one simple line come, short and gentle, nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. If you pray, offer that line to God.

wordCard.voice: Benedict. The young man who left Rome for a cave, and wrote a rule of life that begins with one word: listen.

orig.note: Latin: listen. the first word of the Rule of Benedict.

carryVoice: Your line: listen, with the ear of the heart. One word, and a whole way of life after it. Day seven hundred eighty-six, done.
